Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BOSTON, Massachusetts (CNN)  -- The operator of a trolley that rear-ended another trolley should have been able to see the other vehicle was stopped 480 feet ahead, a federal investigator said Monday. Passengers walk past firefighters at a Green Line station in Boston after the trolley collision Friday evening. The trolley driver has told investigators he was text messaging during Friday night's collision, which injured 20 people. The Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority, which previously had banned operators from using cell phones and other portable devices, now has told employees to leave the devices at home while on duty, National Transportation Safety Board member Debbie Hersman said Monday. Hersman also noted investigators have determined that the operator may have missed some crucial indications of a stopped trolley ahead on the tracks.  Watch new transit rule on cell phones » . "There were several signals -- two green signals, a yellow signal and a red signal -- coming out of the station, and the point of collision occurred 80 feet past that red signal," Hersman said. "We did a site-distance test, and we know that the operator had the ability to see the trolley stopped in front of him 480 feet in advance of the collision." Boston officials said over the weekend that the trolley operator was using his cell phone. Numerous media outlets, including CNN's Boston affiliates, have identified the driver as 24-year-old Aiden Quinn. "The operator of the striking train was interviewed at the hospital by two detectives," said MBTA general manager Daniel Grabauskas. "He admitted that he was texting at the time of the accident." The operator told detectives that, when he looked up, "it was too late as he applied the brake and the train struck the other trolley," Grabauskas said. He described himself as "outraged." "We have reinforced for a number of years that the use of cell phones or any other kinds of electronic devices while operating a train or a bus is absolutely prohibited," Grabauskas said. Though the investigation is ongoing, he said, the two-year employee will be fired if his version of events is confirmed. None of the injuries was considered life-threatening, the MBTA said. The collision happened at 7:18 p.m. ET Friday as the Green Line trains were traveling between the Park Street and Government Center stations in downtown Boston. Both trains were traveling westbound when one train rear-ended the second, an MBTA official said. A train operator also was text messaging last year in a California train crash that killed 25 people. CNN's Rob Frehse and Gary Bender contributed to this report.

Passengers walked past firefighters at a Green Line station in Boston after the trolley collision Friday evening. The trolley driver has told investigators he was text messaging during Friday night’s collision, which injured 20 people.

The Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority, which had previously banned operators from using cell phones and other portable devices, has now instructed employees to leave those devices at home while on duty, National Transportation Safety Board member Debbie Hersman said Monday.

Boston officials said over the weekend that the trolley operator was using his cell phone. Numerous media outlets, including CNN’s Boston affiliates, have identified the driver as 24-year-old Aiden Quinn.

“The operator of the striking train was interviewed at the hospital by two detectives,” said MBTA General Manager Daniel Grabauskas. “He admitted that he was texting at the time of the accident.”

The operator told detectives that when he looked up, “it was too late as he applied the brake and the train struck the other trolley,” Grabauskas said. He described himself as “outraged.”

“We have reinforced for a number of years that the use of cell phones or any other kinds of electronic devices while operating a train or a bus is absolutely prohibited,” Grabauskas said.

Although the investigation is ongoing, Grabauskas said the two-year employee will be fired if his version of events is confirmed.

None of the injuries was considered life-threatening, the MBTA said.

The collision occurred at 7:18 p.m. ET Friday as the Green Line trains were traveling between the Park Street and Government Center stations in downtown Boston. Both trains were traveling westbound when one train rear-ended the other, an MBTA official said.

BOSTON, Massachusetts (CNN) — A federal investigator said Monday that the trolley operator who crashed into the back of another trolley should have been able to spot the stopped train 480 feet before impact.

After Friday evening’s collision on Boston’s Green Line, passengers passed firefighters at a station. The trolley operator has told investigators that he was sending text messages when the crash occurred Friday night, injuring 20 people.

According to National Transportation Safety Board member Debbie Hersman, the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority had already prohibited train and bus operators from using cell phones and other portable electronic devices. Since the crash, the agency has gone further, instructing employees not to bring the devices to work while on duty.

Hersman said investigators also believe the operator may have failed to notice important warning signs indicating there was a trolley stopped ahead on the tracks.

“There were several signals — two green signals, a yellow signal and a red signal — coming out of the station, and the point of collision occurred 80 feet past that red signal,” Hersman said. “We did a site-distance test, and we know that the operator had the ability to see the trolley stopped in front of him 480 feet in advance of the collision.”

Over the weekend, Boston officials said the trolley operator had been using his cell phone. Several news organizations, including CNN affiliates in Boston, have identified him as 24-year-old Aiden Quinn.

MBTA General Manager Daniel Grabauskas said two detectives questioned the operator at the hospital. “He admitted that he was texting at the time of the accident,” Grabauskas said.

The operator told detectives that by the time he looked up, “it was too late as he applied the brake and the train struck the other trolley,” Grabauskas said. He added that he was “outraged.”

“For a number of years, we have made it clear that using cell phones or any other electronic devices while operating a train or bus is strictly forbidden,” Grabauskas said.

Although the investigation has not yet been completed, Grabauskas said the operator, who had worked for the agency for two years, would be dismissed if his account is verified.

The MBTA said none of the injuries appeared to be life-threatening.

The crash took place at 7:18 p.m. ET Friday while Green Line trains were moving between the Park Street and Government Center stations in downtown Boston. An MBTA official said both trains were headed west when one struck the rear of the other.

A train operator was also texting last year during a California rail crash that left 25 people dead.

CNN’s Rob Frehse and Gary Bender contributed to this report.

Passengers described a sudden impact that threw people forward and caused panic inside the trolley.

“It felt like we were hit out of nowhere,” one rider said. “People were screaming, and some were on the floor.”

The collision has renewed scrutiny of safety practices on the Green Line, where trolleys often operate close together in tunnels and along street-level tracks.
